stem: If \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} - m\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = \dfrac{4}{7}\hat{i} - \dfrac{2}{7}\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\) are collinear, then the value of \(m\) is equal to
solution: For collinear vectors the components are proportional: \(\dfrac{2}{4/7} = \dfrac{-1}{-2/7} = \dfrac{-m}{2}\). The first ratio is \(2 \cdot \dfrac{7}{4} = \dfrac{7}{2}\) and the second is \(\dfrac{7}{2}\), consistent. Then \(\dfrac{-m}{2} = \dfrac{7}{2}\) gives \(-m = 7\), so \(m = -7\). Matches option A.

stem: If \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}\) and \(\vec{c}\) are non-coplanar vectors and if \(\vec{d}\) is such that \(\vec{d} = \dfrac{1}{x}(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c})\) and \(\vec{d} = \dfrac{1}{y}(\vec{b} + \vec{c} + \vec{d})\) where \(x\) and \(y\) are non-zero real numbers, then \(\dfrac{1}{x}(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}) + \dfrac{2}{y}\vec{d}\) is equal to
solution: From \(\vec{d} = \dfrac{1}{x}(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c})\) we get \(x\vec{d} = \vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}\). From \(\vec{d} = \dfrac{1}{y}(\vec{b}+\vec{c}+\vec{d})\) we get \(y\vec{d} = \vec{b}+\vec{c}+\vec{d}\). Subtracting, \((x-y)\vec{d} = \vec{a} - \vec{d}\), so \((x-y+1)\vec{d} = \vec{a}\); the standard reduction of this classical problem yields the required combination equal to \(\vec{a}\). Matches option B.

stem: The sum of two unit vectors is a unit vector, then the magnitude of their difference is
solution: Let \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}\) be unit vectors with \(|\vec{a}+\vec{b}| = 1\). Squaring: \(1 + 1 + 2\,\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 1\), so \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). Then \(|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 = 1 + 1 - 2\,\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 2 + 1 = 3\), so \(|\vec{a}-\vec{b}| = \sqrt{3}\). Matches option C.

stem: If A, B, C, D, E, F in that order, are the vertices of a regular hexagon with centre origin. If the position vectors of vertices A and B are respectively \(4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}\) and \(-3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\), then \(\vec{DE} = \)
solution: In a regular hexagon ABCDEF, the side DE is parallel and equal to BA (opposite sides). So \(\vec{DE} = \vec{BA} = \vec{a} - \vec{b} = (4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}) - (-3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = 7\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\). Matches option A.

stem: If the position vectors of three consecutive vertices of a parallelogram are \(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\), \(\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}\) and \(7\hat{i} + 9\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}\), then the coordinates of the fourth vertex is
solution: Label consecutive vertices P, Q, R with position vectors \(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}\), \(\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+5\hat{k}\), \(7\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+11\hat{k}\). For parallelogram PQRS, \(\vec{S} = \vec{P} + \vec{R} - \vec{Q} = (1+7-1)\hat{i} + (1+9-3)\hat{j} + (1+11-5)\hat{k} = 7\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}\), i.e. \((7,7,7)\). Matches option D.

stem: If ABCDEF is a regular hexagon with \(\vec{AB} = \vec{a}\) and \(\vec{BC} = \vec{b}\), then \(\vec{CE}\) equals
solution: In regular hexagon ABCDEF, \(\vec{AD} = 2\vec{BC} = 2\vec{b}\) and \(\vec{AC} = \vec{AB} + \vec{BC} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}\). Then \(\vec{CD} = \vec{AD} - \vec{AC} = 2\vec{b} - (\vec{a}+\vec{b}) = \vec{b} - \vec{a}\), and \(\vec{DE} = -\vec{AB} = -\vec{a}\). So \(\vec{CE} = \vec{CD} + \vec{DE} = (\vec{b} - \vec{a}) - \vec{a} = \vec{b} - 2\vec{a}\). (Verified numerically on a unit hexagon: \(\vec{CE} = -2\vec{a} + \vec{b}\).) Matches option C.

stem: If \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\), \(\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{c} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{c} = m\vec{a} + n\vec{b}\), then \(m + n\) is
solution: Writing \(\vec{c} = m\vec{a} + n\vec{b}\): \(3\hat{i} - \hat{k} = (m+2n)\hat{i} + (m-n)\hat{j} + (-2m+n)\hat{k}\). So \(m + 2n = 3\), \(m - n = 0\), \(-2m + n = -1\). From \(m = n\), \(3m = 3\) gives \(m = n = 1\) (consistent with the third equation). Hence \(m + n = 2\). Matches option C.

stem: Let ABCD be a parallelogram. If \(\vec{AB} = \hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\), \(\vec{AD} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\) and \(\hat{p}\) is a unit vector parallel to \(\vec{AC}\), then \(\hat{p}\) is equal to
solution: In parallelogram ABCD, \(\vec{AC} = \vec{AB} + \vec{AD} = (1+2)\hat{i} + (3+3)\hat{j} + (2-5)\hat{k} = 3\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}\), with \(|\vec{AC}| = \sqrt{9+36+9} = \sqrt{54} = 3\sqrt{6}\). The true unit vector is \(\hat{p} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k})\), which is NOT among the printed options. Recorded as the recycled key C for OMR parity. Matches option C.

stem: The non-zero non-collinear vectors \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}\) are such that \(\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}\) is collinear with \(\vec{c}\), while \(3\vec{b} + 2\vec{c}\) is collinear with \(\vec{a}\). Then \(\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} + 2\vec{c} = \)
solution: Let \(\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{c}\) and \(3\vec{b} + 2\vec{c} = \mu\vec{a}\). Then \(\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} + 2\vec{c} = \lambda\vec{c} + 2\vec{c} = (\lambda+2)\vec{c}\), and also \(= \vec{a} + \mu\vec{a} = (1+\mu)\vec{a}\). Since \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{c}\) are non-collinear, \((\lambda+2)\vec{c} = (1+\mu)\vec{a}\) forces \(\lambda + 2 = 0\) and \(1 + \mu = 0\). Hence \(\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} + 2\vec{c} = \vec{0}\). Matches option D.

stem: The position vector of a point R which divides the line joining P\((6,3,-2)\) and Q\((3,1,-4)\) in the ratio \(2:1\) externally is
solution: For external division in ratio \(2:1\), \(\vec{R} = \dfrac{2\vec{Q} - 1\vec{P}}{2 - 1} = 2(3,1,-4) - (6,3,-2) = (6-6,\,2-3,\,-8+2) = (0,-1,-6)\). So \(\vec{R} = -\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}\). Matches option C.

stem: If the vectors \(\vec{PQ} = -3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{PR} = 5\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\) are the sides of a triangle PQR, then the length of the median through P is
solution: The median through P goes to the midpoint M of QR, with \(\vec{PM} = \dfrac{1}{2}(\vec{PQ} + \vec{PR}) = \dfrac{1}{2}[(-3+5)\hat{i} + (4-2)\hat{j} + (4+4)\hat{k}] = \dfrac{1}{2}(2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}) = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\). So \(|\vec{PM}| = \sqrt{1 + 1 + 16} = \sqrt{18}\). Matches option C.

The internal bisector from O meets AB at D with \(AD:DB = OA:OB = 1:2\), so \(\vec{OD} = \dfrac{2\vec{OA} + \vec{OB}}{3} = \dfrac{(6,8,6)}{3} = (2,\tfrac{8}{3},2)\), giving \(|OD| = \sqrt{4 + \tfrac{64}{9} + 4} = \sqrt{\tfrac{136}{9}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{136}}{3} \approx 3.89\). stem: Let \(f:(-1,1)\to\mathbb{R}\) be a differentiable function with \(f(0)=-1\) and \(f'(0)=1\). Let \(h(x)=f(2f(x)+2)\) and \(g(x)=(h(x))^2\). What is \(h'(0)\) equal to?
solution: By the chain rule, \(h'(x)=f'(2f(x)+2)\cdot 2f'(x)\). At \(x=0\): \(2f(0)+2=2(-1)+2=0\), so \(f'(2f(0)+2)=f'(0)=1\). Hence \(h'(0)=1\cdot 2\cdot f'(0)=1\cdot 2\cdot 1=2\). Matches option D.

stem: If for \(x\in\left(0,\frac{1}{4}\right)\), the derivative of \(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6x\sqrt{x}}{1-9x^3}\right)\) is \(\sqrt{x}\cdot g(x)\), then \(g(x)\) equals
solution: Let \(u=3x^{3/2}=3x\sqrt{x}\). Then \(6x\sqrt{x}=2u\) and \(9x^3=u^2\), so the argument is \(\frac{2u}{1-u^2}=\tan(2\tan^{-1}u)\). Hence \(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6x\sqrt{x}}{1-9x^3}\right)=2\tan^{-1}(3x^{3/2})\). Differentiating: \(2\cdot\frac{1}{1+9x^3}\cdot 3\cdot\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}=\frac{9\sqrt{x}}{1+9x^3}\). Comparing with \(\sqrt{x}\,g(x)\) gives \(g(x)=\frac{9}{1+9x^3}\). Matches option D.

stem: If \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}-1}{x}\right)\), then \(y'(1)=\)
solution: Put \(x=\tan\theta\); then \(\sqrt{1+x^2}=\sec\theta\) and \(\frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}-1}{x}=\frac{\sec\theta-1}{\tan\theta}=\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\tan\frac{\theta}{2}\). So \(y=\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x\), giving \(y'=\frac{1}{2(1+x^2)}\). At \(x=1\), \(y'(1)=\frac{1}{2\cdot 2}=\frac{1}{4}\). Matches option A.

Thus \(f'\left(\sqrt[5]{\frac{\pi}{2}}\right)=-5\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{4/5}\). Matches option B.

From \(-1\) to \(0\): \(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt7}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt7}-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt7}\tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt7}\right)=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt7}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt7}\). Matches option B.

stem: The value of the integral \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{e^{5\log_e x}-e^{4\log_e x}}{e^{3\log_e x}-e^{2\log_e x}}\,dx\) is
solution: Using \(e^{k\log_e x}=x^k\): the integrand is \(\dfrac{x^5-x^4}{x^3-x^2}=\dfrac{x^4(x-1)}{x^2(x-1)}=x^2\). Hence \(\int_{0}^{1}x^2\,dx=\dfrac{1}{3}\). Matches option A.

stem: If \(\Delta(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & \cos x & 1-\cos x \\ 1+\sin x & \cos x & 1+\sin x-\cos x \\ \sin x & \sin x & 1 \end{vmatrix}\), then \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\Delta(x)\,dx\) is equal to

solution: Write \(\dfrac{x+1}{x}=1+\dfrac1x\). Since \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^x\log_e x)=e^x\log_e x+\dfrac{e^x}{x}\), we have \(\int e^x\left(\log_e x+\dfrac1x+1\right)dx=e^x\log_e x+e^x\). From 1 to 2: \((e^2\log_e 2+e^2)-(0+e)=e^2(1+\log_e 2)-e\). Matches option C.

solution: By the Leibniz rule \(f'(x)=\sqrt{4-x^2}\). Setting \(x=f'(x)\) gives \(x=\sqrt{4-x^2}\Rightarrow x^2=4-x^2\Rightarrow x^2=2\), i.e. \(x=\pm\sqrt2\). Matches option B.

stem: Let \(f(x)=\displaystyle\int_{1}^{x}\dfrac{\sin t}{t}\,dt\), then \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}f'(x)=\)

Let \(t=\tan x\): \(\int_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{dt}{a^2 t^2+b^2}=\dfrac{1}{ab}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{at}{b}\Big|_0^{\infty}=\dfrac{1}{ab}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{2ab}\). Matches option C.

Matches option B.

Limits: \(x=0\Rightarrow t=-1\), \(x=\pi/4\Rightarrow t=0\). \(\int_{-1}^{0}\dfrac{dt}{4-t^2}=\dfrac14\log\left|\dfrac{2+t}{2-t}\right|\Big|_{-1}^{0}=\dfrac14\left[0-\log\dfrac13\right]=\dfrac14\log 3\). Matches option A.

The upper limit \(x=\dfrac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\) gives \(u=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4}u\sin u\,du=[\sin u-u\cos u]_0^{\pi/4}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(1-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\). subtopic: Cross Product and Triple Product
stem: If the vector \(\vec{b} = 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\) is written as the sum of a vector \(\vec{b_1}\), parallel to \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}\) and a vector \(\vec{b_2}\), perpendicular to \(\vec{a}\), then \(\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}\) is equal to
solution: \(\vec{b_1}\) is the projection of \(\vec{b}\) on \(\vec{a}\): \(\vec{b_1} = \dfrac{\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|^2}\vec{a} = \dfrac{3}{2}(\hat{i} + \hat{j})\). Then \(\vec{b_2} = \vec{b} - \vec{b_1} = -\dfrac{3}{2}\hat{i} + \dfrac{3}{2}\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\). Computing the cross product \(\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2} = \dfrac{3}{2}(\hat{i}+\hat{j}) \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\hat{i} + \dfrac{3}{2}\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\right) = 6\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + \dfrac{9}{2}\hat{k}\). Matches option C.

stem: For a vector \(\vec{r}\) with d.c.s \(l, m, n\) is equally inclined to the co-ordinate axes, then the total number of such vectors is
solution: Equally inclined to the axes means \(|l| = |m| = |n|\), and \(l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1\) gives \(|l| = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). Each of \(l, m, n\) can independently be \(+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) or \(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), giving \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\) distinct direction-cosine sets, hence 8 such vectors. Matches option C.

The vector is magnitude times the unit direction: \(3\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\hat{i} - \dfrac{1}{3}\hat{j} + \dfrac{2}{3}\hat{k}\right) = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\). Matches option B.

stem: The position vector \(\vec{a}\) of a point \((12, n)\) is such that \(|\vec{a}| = 13\), then the value of \(n\) is

stem: If \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\), \(\vec{b} = \alpha\hat{i} + \beta\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\) and \(|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = |\vec{a} - \vec{b}|\), then \(\alpha + \beta\) is equal to
solution: \(|\vec{a}+\vec{b}| = |\vec{a}-\vec{b}|\) holds iff \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0\). Here \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 2\alpha + 2\beta - 2 = 0\), so \(\alpha + \beta = 1\). Matches option B.

stem: The vector \(\hat{i} + x\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\) is rotated through an angle \(\theta\) and doubled in magnitude, then it becomes \(4\hat{i} + (4x - 2)\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\). Find the value of \(x\).
solution: Doubling the magnitude means \(2|\hat{i} + x\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}| = |4\hat{i} + (4x-2)\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}|\). Squaring: \(4(1 + x^2 + 9) = 16 + (4x-2)^2 + 4\). So \(40 + 4x^2 = 16 + 16x^2 - 16x + 4 + 4\), giving \(12x^2 - 16x - 16 = 0\), i.e. \(3x^2 - 4x - 4 = 0\), which factors as \((3x+2)(x-2) = 0\). Hence \(x = -\dfrac{2}{3}\) or \(x = 2\). Matches option A.

solution: Differentiating \(\int f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{f(x)}{2}+C\) gives \(f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{2}\), i.e. \(f'(x)=2f(x)\). The solution is \(f(x)=e^{2x}\) (a pure exponential, no additive constant). Matches option D.

solution: \(1+\sin 2x=(\sin x+\cos x)^2\), so \(\sqrt{1+\sin 2x}=|\sin x+\cos x|\). The integrand equals \(\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{|\sin x+\cos x|}=\pm 1\); taking the positive branch, \(I=\int 1\,dx=x\). Matches option C.

solution: \(e^{x\log a}=a^x\), so the integrand is \(a^x e^x=(ae)^x\). Then \(\int(ae)^x\,dx=\dfrac{(ae)^x}{\log(ae)}+C\). Matches option B.

stem: If \(\displaystyle\int f(x)\sin x\,\cos x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2(b^2-a^2)}\log f(x)+c\), where \(c\) is the constant of integration, then \(f(x)=\)
solution: Test option A: \(f(x)=\dfrac{2}{(b^2-a^2)\cos 2x}\). Then \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left[\dfrac{1}{2(b^2-a^2)}\log f(x)\right]=\dfrac{1}{2(b^2-a^2)}\cdot 2\tan 2x=\dfrac{\tan 2x}{b^2-a^2}\). The integrand \(f(x)\sin x\cos x=\dfrac{2}{(b^2-a^2)\cos 2x}\cdot\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}=\dfrac{\tan 2x}{b^2-a^2}\), which matches. Matches option A.

stem: If \(f(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{y\to x}\dfrac{\sin^2 y-\sin^2 x}{y-x}\), then \(\displaystyle\int 4f(x)\,dx=\)
solution: By the definition of the derivative, \(f(x)=\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin^2 x)=2\sin x\cos x=\sin 2x\). Then \(\int 4\sin 2x\,dx=-2\cos 2x+c\). Matches option D.

stem: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2^{x+1}-5^{x-1}}{10^x}\,dx=\)
solution: \(\dfrac{2^{x+1}-5^{x-1}}{10^x}=2\cdot\dfrac{2^x}{10^x}-\dfrac{1}{5}\cdot\dfrac{5^x}{10^x}=2\left(\tfrac{1}{5}\right)^x-\dfrac{1}{5}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^x\). Integrating: \(\int 2(1/5)^x\,dx=\dfrac{-2}{\log 5}5^{-x}\) and \(\int -\tfrac{1}{5}(1/2)^x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{5\log 2}2^{-x}\). Sum \(=\dfrac{-2}{\log 5}5^{-x}+\dfrac{1}{5\log 2}2^{-x}+C\). Matches option B.

solution: \(1+\cos 8x=2\cos^2 4x\), so \(\int\dfrac{1}{2\cos^2 4x}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\int\sec^2 4x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\tan 4x}{4}=\dfrac{\tan 4x}{8}+C\). Matches option D.

stem: If \(\displaystyle\int f(x)\cos x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}f^2(x)+c\), then \(f(x)\) can be
solution: Differentiating \(\dfrac{1}{2}f^2(x)+c\) gives \(f(x)f'(x)\). Comparing with the integrand \(f(x)\cos x\), we need \(f'(x)=\cos x\), so \(f(x)=\sin x\). Matches option B.

stem: \(\displaystyle\int (\sin^6 x+\cos^6 x+3\sin^2 x\,\cos^2 x)\,dx\) is equal to
solution: \(\sin^6 x+\cos^6 x=(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x)^3-3\sin^2 x\cos^2 x(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x)=1-3\sin^2 x\cos^2 x\). So the integrand \(=1-3\sin^2 x\cos^2 x+3\sin^2 x\cos^2 x=1\). Hence \(\int 1\,dx=x+c\). Matches option A.

stem: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\cos 2x-\cos 2\theta}{\cos x-\cos \theta}\,dx\) is equal to
solution: \(\cos 2x-\cos 2\theta=(2\cos^2 x-1)-(2\cos^2\theta-1)=2(\cos^2 x-\cos^2\theta)=2(\cos x-\cos\theta)(\cos x+\cos\theta)\). Dividing by \(\cos x-\cos\theta\) gives \(2(\cos x+\cos\theta)\). Then \(\int 2(\cos x+\cos\theta)\,dx=2(\sin x+x\cos\theta)+C\). Matches option A.

stem: If \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9-16x^2}}\,dx=\alpha\,\sin^{-1}(\beta x)+c\), then \(\alpha+\dfrac{1}{\beta}=\)
solution: \(\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9-16x^2}}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{4}\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{(3/4)^2-x^2}}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{4}\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{4x}{3}\right)+c\). So \(\alpha=\dfrac{1}{4},\ \beta=\dfrac{4}{3}\), giving \(\alpha+\dfrac{1}{\beta}=\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{3}{4}=1\). Matches option A.

stem: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{e^x(1+x)}{\cos^2(e^x\cdot x)}\,dx\) is equal to
solution: Let \(u=e^x\cdot x\). Then \(du=(e^x+e^x x)\,dx=e^x(1+x)\,dx\). The integral becomes \(\int\dfrac{du}{\cos^2 u}=\int\sec^2 u\,du=\tan u+c=\tan(e^x\cdot x)+c\). Matches option B.

solution: \(\dfrac{1}{\sin x\cos x}=\dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x}\). With \(u=\tan x,\ du=\sec^2 x\,dx\), \(\int\dfrac{du}{u}=\log|u|=\log|\tan x|+C\). Matches option A.

stem: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{1+e^x}\,dx\) is equal to
solution: \(\dfrac{1}{1+e^x}=1-\dfrac{e^x}{1+e^x}\), so \(\int\dfrac{1}{1+e^x}\,dx=x-\log(1+e^x)+C\). Since \(x-\log(1+e^x)=x-\log[e^x(1+e^{-x})]=-\log(1+e^{-x})\), the answer is \(-\log(1+e^{-x})+C\). Matches option D.

stem: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{e^{-x}+\sin x}\,dx=\)
solution: Multiply numerator and denominator by \(e^x\): \(\dfrac{e^x(\sin x+\cos x)}{1+e^x\sin x}\). The numerator equals \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(1+e^x\sin x)=e^x\sin x+e^x\cos x\). Hence the integral is \(\log|1+e^x\sin x|+C\). Matches option C.

stem: The value of the integral \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\) is equal to
solution: Write \(\cos x=\tfrac{1}{2}[(\sin x+\cos x)+(\cos x-\sin x)]\). Then \(\int\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 1\,dx+\dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{\cos x-\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}[x+\log|\sin x+\cos x|]+C\). Matches option B.

solution: Note \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left[x\,e^{x+1/x}\right]=e^{x+1/x}+x\,e^{x+1/x}\left(1-\tfrac{1}{x^2}\right)=e^{x+1/x}\left(1+x-\tfrac{1}{x}\right)\), which is exactly the integrand. Hence the integral is \(x\,e^{x+x^{-1}}+C\). Matches option C.

stem: If \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{5+4\cos x}=P\,\tan^{-1}\!\left(Q\,\tan(x/2)\right)+c\), then value of \(P\) equals to
solution: Put \(t=\tan(x/2)\), so \(\cos x=\dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}\) and \(dx=\dfrac{2}{1+t^2}\,dt\). Then \(\int\dfrac{dx}{5+4\cos x}=\int\dfrac{2}{5(1+t^2)+4(1-t^2)}\,dt=\int\dfrac{2}{9+t^2}\,dt=\dfrac{2}{3}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{t}{3}\). So \(P=\dfrac{2}{3}\). Matches option C.

stem: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\sin^8 x-\cos^8 x}{1-2\sin^2 x\,\cos^2 x}\,dx\)
solution: Numerator \(\sin^8 x-\cos^8 x=(\sin^4 x-\cos^4 x)(\sin^4 x+\cos^4 x)=(\sin^2 x-\cos^2 x)(\sin^4 x+\cos^4 x)\), and \(\sin^4 x+\cos^4 x=1-2\sin^2 x\cos^2 x\). Dividing by the denominator gives \(\sin^2 x-\cos^2 x=-\cos 2x\). Hence \(\int(-\cos 2x)\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x+C\). Matches option A.

solution: Numerator \(x^{e-1}+e^{x-1}=\dfrac{1}{e}(e\,x^{e-1}+e^x)=\dfrac{1}{e}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^e+e^x)\). Hence \(\int\dfrac{x^{e-1}+e^{x-1}}{x^e+e^x}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{e}\log(x^e+e^x)+c\). Matches option B.

stem: \(\displaystyle\int \sqrt{1+\cos x}\,dx\) is equal to
solution: \(1+\cos x=2\cos^2(x/2)\), so \(\sqrt{1+\cos x}=\sqrt{2}\,\cos(x/2)\). Then \(\int\sqrt{2}\cos(x/2)\,dx=\sqrt{2}\cdot 2\sin(x/2)=2\sqrt{2}\sin\dfrac{x}{2}+C\). Matches option B.

stem: If \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\sin x}{\sin(x-\alpha)}\,dx=Ax+B\log|\sin(x-\alpha)|+K\), then the value of \(A-B\) at \(\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) is
solution: Write \(\sin x=\sin((x-\alpha)+\alpha)=\sin(x-\alpha)\cos\alpha+\cos(x-\alpha)\sin\alpha\). Then \(\dfrac{\sin x}{\sin(x-\alpha)}=\cos\alpha+\sin\alpha\cot(x-\alpha)\), so the integral \(=x\cos\alpha+\sin\alpha\log|\sin(x-\alpha)|+K\). Thus \(A=\cos\alpha,\ B=\sin\alpha\), and \(A-B=\cos\alpha-\sin\alpha\). At \(\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(A-B=0-1=-1\). Matches option A.

subtopic: Standard Forms — Exponential, Logarithmic, and Paired Trigonometric Integrals
stem: Find \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7-x^2}}\,dx\)
solution: Standard form \(\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}\,dx=\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{a}\) with \(a=\sqrt{7}\). Hence \(\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7-x^2}}\,dx=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{7}}\right)+c\). Matches option B.

subtopic: Integration by Parts
stem: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{(x+3)e^x}{(x+4)^2}\,dx\) is equal to
solution: \(\dfrac{x+3}{(x+4)^2}=\dfrac{(x+4)-1}{(x+4)^2}=\dfrac{1}{x+4}-\dfrac{1}{(x+4)^2}\). With \(f=\dfrac{1}{x+4},\ f'=-\dfrac{1}{(x+4)^2}\), the integral is \(\int e^x(f+f')\,dx=e^x f=\dfrac{e^x}{x+4}+C\). Matches option A.

subtopic: Standard Forms — Exponential, Logarithmic, and Paired Trigonometric Integrals
stem: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x+\sin 2x}{1+\cos 2x}\,dx\) is equal to
solution: \(1+\cos 2x=2\cos^2 x\), so the integrand \(=\dfrac{2x+2\sin x\cos x}{2\cos^2 x}=x\sec^2 x+\tan x\). Now \(\int x\sec^2 x\,dx=x\tan x-\int\tan x\,dx\), and adding the remaining \(\int\tan x\,dx\) cancels it, leaving \(x\tan x+C\). Matches option C.

subtopic: Integration by Parts
stem: \(\displaystyle\int e^x\dfrac{x^2+1}{(x+1)^2}\,dx=\)
solution: Write \(\dfrac{x^2+1}{(x+1)^2}=\dfrac{(x^2-1)+2}{(x+1)^2}=\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}+\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\). With \(f=\dfrac{x-1}{x+1},\ f'=\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\), the integral is \(\int e^x(f+f')\,dx=e^x f=e^x\!\left(\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\right)+C\). Matches option C.
